title: Why Elevators Mattered
objective: After this level you can explain how safe elevators made tall buildings possible.
summary: Otis's 1854 safety brake and the 1857 passenger elevator made buildings over four or five stories practical, and turned the attic of the poor into the prized penthouse.

cards.headline: A few seconds in 1854 decided which floor would be the best one.
cards.body: At New York's Crystal Palace, Elisha Otis rode his raised elevator platform in front of a crowd and had its rope cut. The platform held. That little stunt ended up changing what buildings looked like, and who lived at the top.

cards.headline: A brake the rope switches on
cards.body: Otis's safety device gripped the guide rails the moment the hoist rope lost its tension, so a snapped rope set the brake all by itself. In 1857 the first safe passenger elevator went into the E.V. Haughwout store in New York City. It made buildings of more than four or five stories practical. Before that, the limit on a building's height was your legs.

cards.headline: The top floor gets promoted
cards.body: Before elevators, the attic was an awkward climb, the retreat of the poor. New York's Equitable Life Assurance Building, finished in 1870, is said to be the city's first office building with a passenger elevator, and it made its upper floors as convenient as the lower ones, and even more desirable. By the 1920s the old attic had become the sought-after penthouse.

mascot.line: Same top floor, same view. The only thing that changed was the ride up.

cards.fact: The elevator helped draw the modern city.
cards.context: By opening the way to higher buildings, the elevator played a decisive role in creating the urban geography of many modern cities. Remember Level 61's first skyscrapers, with steel frames and elevators? The frame let a building stand tall. The elevator made its upper floors worth having.

cards.headline: Elevators: going up
learned: Otis, 1854: the rope was cut and the platform held
His brake gripped the guide rails when the rope went slack
1857: safe passenger elevators made 5+ story buildings practical
Elevators turned the attic into the penthouse

questions.prompt: What did the 1857 passenger elevator in New York's Haughwout store make practical?

options.label: Iron and glass exhibition halls
options.rationale: The Crystal Palace was where Otis demonstrated, not what the elevator made practical.

options.label: Buildings of more than four or five stories
Houses with deep basements
options.rationale: It was about going up, not down.

options.label: Brick walls thicker at the bottom
options.rationale: Thick walls were the old way to go tall, not the elevator's gift.

questions.explanation: The first safe passenger elevator (1857) made buildings of more than four or five stories practical.

questions.prompt: Why did the top floor go from the attic of the poor to the sought-after penthouse?

options.label: Elevators made upper floors as easy to reach as lower ones
New laws banned homes on lower floors
options.rationale: No law did it; the elevator did.

options.label: Top floors were rebuilt with thicker walls
options.rationale: Walls weren't the change; access was.

options.label: Stairs in new buildings were made shorter

questions.explanation: Once elevators made upper floors convenient, they became even more desirable than the lower ones.

questions.prompt: Level 8's frame carries a building's floors. What did the elevator add that a frame alone couldn't?

options.label: Resistance to fire
options.rationale: Fire resistance isn't what the elevator gave.

options.label: A way to carry the floors' weight
options.rationale: That's the frame's job, as Level 8 showed.

options.label: Upper floors that people wanted to reach
Walls that could be made of glass
options.rationale: Level 8's frame did that, not the elevator.

questions.explanation: The frame let a building stand tall; the elevator made its upper floors worth having.
